271.quote_or_event: “Outwardly, they wear religious robes, but within is the filth of Maya. They cannot conceal this, no matter how hard they try.”
271.explanation: In the Sukhmani Guru Arjan describes people who wear holy dress over a mind full of worldly filth, and says the truth cannot be hidden however much they try.
271.tie_back: Valluvar pictures the hypocrite's own five elements laughing at his sham holiness; Guru Arjan likewise says the inner corruption under the robe cannot be concealed.
271.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 267, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
271._accuracy_note: Strong fit on sham piety that cannot hide itself, though the Kural's distinctive image of the body's five elements as mocking witnesses is absent.

272.quote_or_event: “Mentally, we are impure and black, but outwardly, we appear white.”
272.explanation: In a salok of Vaar Sri Raag Guru Nanak speaks in the first person for all of us, admitting that our minds are impure and black while we look white and clean outside.
272.tie_back: The Kural asks what use a sky-high holy appearance is when one's own heart knows its faults; Guru Nanak's confession is exactly that inner knowledge of the gap between how we look and what we are.
272.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 85, Vaar Sri Raag (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
272._accuracy_note: Strong fit on outward show versus a heart aware of its own faults, though Guru Nanak's line is a humble confession rather than a rebuke of ascetic garb.

273.quote_or_event: “Fareed, you wear your prayer shawl on your shoulders and the robes of a Sufi; your words are sweet, but there is a dagger in your heart.”
273.explanation: Shaikh Farid rebukes the false holy man who puts on the prayer shawl and robe of a Sufi and talks sweetly while hiding a dagger in his heart.
273.tie_back: Valluvar likens the weak-willed man in an ascetic's fierce form to a cow in a tiger's skin grazing another's crop; Farid's false Sufi likewise uses borrowed holy dress to cover what he really is.
273.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1380, Salok Sheikh Farid 50 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
273._accuracy_note: Reasonable: borrowed holy garb over a different inner nature fits, but the Kural's point is inner weakness hiding behind fierceness, while Farid's is malice hiding behind sweetness.

274.quote_or_event: “The herons in their white feathers dwell in the sacred shrines of pilgrimage. They tear apart and eat the living beings, and so they are not called white.”
274.explanation: In Raag Soohee Guru Nanak points to herons that live at holy bathing places in spotless white while seizing and devouring living creatures.
274.tie_back: Valluvar compares the predator hiding behind the garb of penance to a hunter hiding in a bush to snare birds; Guru Nanak's heron likewise uses a pure-looking appearance in a holy place to catch its prey.
274.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
274._accuracy_note: Close match: a predator hiding behind a pure, holy appearance to catch unsuspecting victims; only the specific image differs (heron rather than fowler in a bush).

275.quote_or_event: “He dyes his robes with saffron dye, and wearing these robes, he goes out begging. … From house to house he goes begging, and tries to teach the world; but his mind is blind, and so he loses his honor.”
275.explanation: In Raag Maaroo Guru Nanak describes a man who puts on the saffron robe of renunciation and begs from door to door, preaching to others while his own mind stays blind, until he loses his honour.
275.tie_back: The Kural warns that those who falsely claim to have given up all attachment will end up crying 'what have we done!'; Guru Nanak likewise shows the false renunciant ending in disgrace.
275.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1012, Raag Maaroo, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
275._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit: the false renunciant comes to grief in both, but loss of honour is milder than the Kural's many sorrows and the cry of regret is absent; the ellipsis marks one omitted line.

276.quote_or_event: “The man-eaters say their prayers. Those who wield the knife wear the sacred thread around their necks.”
276.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak attacks officials of his day who devoured the people and preyed on the poor while making a show of prayer and wearing the sacred thread.
276.tie_back: Valluvar calls none more hard-hearted than those who live by deceiving others while posing as holy; Guru Nanak's man-eaters at prayer show the same cruelty under a religious surface.
276.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 471, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
276._accuracy_note: Strong fit on cruelty hidden behind religious display, though Guru Nanak's targets are corrupt officials and scribes, not false renunciants.

277.quote_or_event: “Bronze is bright and shiny, but when it is rubbed, its blackness appears.”
277.explanation: Guru Nanak opens a hymn in Raag Soohee with the image of polished bronze, bright on the surface but leaving black marks once it is rubbed, as a picture of a person who only looks good.
277.tie_back: Valluvar's kundri seed is bright red outside with a black tip; Guru Nanak's bronze is likewise bright outside and black underneath.
277.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
277._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: a bright object hiding blackness stands for people who are fair outside and dark within; only the object differs (bronze rather than the kundri seed).

278.quote_or_event: “With filth within the heart, even if one bathes at sacred places of pilgrimage, still, he shall not go to heaven.”
278.explanation: Bhagat Kabir declares that a person whose heart is full of filth gains nothing from bathing at holy places of pilgrimage.
278.tie_back: Valluvar mocks those who bathe in sacred waters with filth in their minds and live hidden behind that show; Kabir says the same, that ritual bathing cannot wash an inner filth.
278.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 484, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
278._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on ritual bathing with a filthy mind; Kabir stresses the lack of spiritual benefit rather than the hiding behind it.

279.quote_or_event: “The simmal tree is straight as an arrow; it is very tall, and very thick. … Sweetness and humility, O Nanak, are the essence of virtue and goodness.”
279.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak notes that the silk-cotton tree is straight, tall and imposing, yet birds that come to it leave disappointed, and concludes that sweetness and humility are what make a person good.
279.tie_back: Valluvar says the arrow is straight but cruel and the lute bent but sweet, so people must be judged by their deeds, not their looks; Guru Nanak's straight-as-an-arrow tree yields nothing, while humble sweetness is the real worth.
279.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
279._accuracy_note: Strong fit: both judge by inner worth rather than an imposing straight outline, and even share the arrow image; the ellipsis marks omitted lines about the tree's useless fruit.

280.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, you have not shaved your mind, so why do you shave your head?”
280.explanation: Kabir tells the shaven-headed ascetic that unless the mind itself has been cleared of vice, shaving the head means nothing.
280.tie_back: Valluvar says neither shaving the head nor growing matted hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Kabir likewise says the outward mark is useless without a changed mind.
280.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1369, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
280._accuracy_note: Strong fit on shaving the head, but Sikhs keep uncut hair (kesh) as a mark of commitment, so Sikh practice does not share the Kural's dismissal of long hair even while sharing its stress on inner change.
